title: AI Makes Verifying the Bottleneck with Dave Farley @ModernSoftwareEngineeringYT
summary: Dave Farley argues AI amplifies good engineering practice, that verification through TDD/BDD specifications becomes the bottleneck, and that gains are real but far below 10x.

verdicts.note: The Echoes of AI controlled experiment found no significant maintainability penalty, though it covered one task and small changes.

Preregistered RCT, 75 mostly professional developers manually evolving Java code written with or without AI: no reliable difference in completion time or perceived productivity, and the study is only powered to rule out large effects.

Same RCT on quality: no frequentist CodeHealth difference after a second developer evolved the code, a small Bayesian CodeHealth gain when a habitual AI user wrote the original, and identical test coverage. Scope is limited to a small app and short-term effects.
The mining study of 302k AI-authored commits explicitly has no human-written baseline, so its counts of surviving debt cannot show that AI code is harder to maintain than human code.

11 of 47 sources raise maintainability concerns: conversational code that lacks cohesive structure and documentation, structural complexity from rapid iteration, and long-term debt. These are reported concerns rather than measured comparisons with unassisted code.

The related work cites Borg et al.'s 151-participant controlled experiment, which found no consistent sign that AI-assisted code was harder for later developers to maintain, while warning of cognitive debt. This is secondary evidence; the study's own data cover only the original author.

The follow-up survey linked AI use to lower self-rated maintainability and more technical debt, which points against 'no harder to maintain'. These are self-reports, not measures of later maintainers.
